nameStory: Eris flava gets its genus name from Eris, the Greek goddess of discord and strife, perhaps referencing the aggressive hunting style of these jumping spiders. The species name 'flava' means 'yellow' or 'golden' in Latin, likely referring to some yellowish coloration on the spider's body.
description: Eris flava is a small jumping spider found throughout the eastern United States, including New England. Like all jumping spiders, it has a compact, stocky body with relatively large front-facing eyes that give it excellent vision for hunting. These spiders are active daytime hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead stalking and pouncing on small insects with impressive precision. They typically measure around a quarter to half an inch in body length.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a front-facing row, with the middle pair noticeably larger and giving the spider an almost curious, alert expression when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, stocky build with a relatively flat, rectangular front section (cephalothorax) and robust legs that feel sturdy when the spider walks across your hand

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Males display a distinctive band of white or pale scales across the clypeus (the face area below the eyes), creating a bright stripe that catches sunlight

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often turning to face you directly when approached, and may raise its front legs in a defensive posture

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small silk retreats rather than webs - look for tiny silk-lined crevices or rolled leaves where they rest at night or during bad weather

habitat: Look for Eris flava in sunny, open areas with low vegetation such as meadows, field edges, and garden borders where they hunt on flowers and low shrubs. They prefer areas with some structure like tall grasses or herbaceous plants that provide both hunting grounds and shelter. These spiders are often found basking on sun-warmed surfaces like fence posts, rocks, or wooden structures.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter shelters to begin hunting and mating. Look for males displaying their white facial stripes during courtship rituals.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both adults and juveniles are most visible hunting during warm, sunny days. Females may be seen guarding their silk egg sacs in protected locations.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues through early fall as spiders bulk up for winter, with juveniles from summer egg laying becoming more noticeable as they grow larger.
seasonality.winter: Adults seek shelter under bark, in leaf litter, or other protected spots where they remain dormant until spring temperatures return.

funFact: Despite having eight eyes total, jumping spiders like Eris flava have better color vision than most mammals and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, allowing them to detect patterns on flowers and prey that are completely invisible to human eyes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Bronze Jumping Spider (Eris militaris), but male Eris flava can be distinguished by the bright white band of scales across their face below the eyes - if you see this facial 'headband,' you've found flava rather than militaris.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, Eris flava appears to be quite rare in our region, making any sighting particularly noteworthy. This spider is much more common in the southern United States, so New England represents the northern edge of its range.
compareHints: Eris flava is very similar to its close relative the Bronze Jumping Spider (Eris militaris), but males can be reliably separated by the white facial band that militaris lacks. Both species share the same general body shape, size, and hunting behavior, but flava appears to be much less common in New England. The white facial markings on male flava are distinctive enough that once you know what to look for, identification becomes straightforward.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bronze Jumping Spiders can be distinguished from their relatives in the Eris genus by their distinctive bronze coloration and the female's white-spotted abdomen pattern.

Eris floridana is very similar to its relatives the Bronze Jumping Spider (Eris militaris) and Eris flava, and reliable identification often requires close examination of body markings and proportions.
